item.title: How Wall Street Is Pitching Anthropic’s I.P.O.: ‘Too Crucial to Fail’
item.description:
On Friday afternoon, on the 56th floor of JPMorgan’s headquarters, Jamie Dimon interviewed perhaps the most important man to Wall Street right now: Dario Amodei, the chief executive of Anthropic.

With less than one week before Anthropic plans to sell its shares on the open market, both men projected calm and confidence heading into what could be the largest initial public offering ever.

“We’re not super fussed on when exactly, what month, or what day, or what market conditions we go public into,” Dr. Amodei said, speaking on a small stage as thick clouds enveloped the New York skyline behind him.

Dr. Amodei’s nonchalance, though, belies the intensity of Wall Street’s efforts to sell Anthropic to investors. The company has lined up 22 banks, led by Goldman Sachs and Morgan Stanley, to run its “roadshow,” a series of meetings and presentations, where investors hear about the company’s financials.

Anthropic disclosed earlier this week it aimed to raise up to $100 billion at a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion, down from $2 trillion bankers had floated this summer, before market jitters appeared.

JPMorgan and Citi are stewarding efforts to sell to individual investors, which Anthropic has said it expects to make up about 20 percent of the offering. Another critical group of investors: Seven of the tech industry’s biggest players, including Broadcom, Nvidia and Microsoft, which have already signed up to invest a total of $26 billion in Anthropic immediately after listing.

Each of those seven technology firms also stands to benefit from a successful Anthropic listing: Some, like Nvidia, Google and Microsoft, were already investors. All of them count Anthropic as a customer, and a successful Anthropic offering means a sustainable buyer of their services.

And the banks themselves could stand to collect roughly $400 million in fees on the deal, according to analysts at Evercore.

Anthropic is entering a market that has been less than ideal. Concerns about debt-fueled spending on artificial intelligence have whipsawed stock and bond prices for weeks. This week’s shocking resignation of Jensen Huang as Nvidia’s chief executive added more turmoil and uncertainty.

“Everyone has an interest in making this a success,” said Craig Coben, a former global head of equity capital markets at Bank of America, describing Anthropic’s offering as “too crucial to fail.”

“So far the market thinks the A.I. ecosystem can withstand Huang’s resignation,” Mr. Coben said, “but it’s still processing in real time what it all means for future spend and investment.”

Throughout its roadshow, Anthropic’s messaging has been that it will try to control its own destiny. In private meetings in New York conference rooms and on video calls, executives have stressed to investors that the company will rise above the fray by using a new cash pile from the I.P.O. to develop its own chips and build their own data centers.

They’re also selling what is, for now, a dream. Dr. Amodei has spent significant time in meetings on a subject without much traction yet: the company’s early forays into helping to develop new drugs and automate science laboratories, two investors said.

Anthropic, and its advisers, have taken a notably more austere approach than Elon Musk’s SpaceX public offering in June, a reflection in part of Dr. Amodei’s more understated style.

Mr. Musk’s roadshow video that opened with orchestral music, a snapshot of the moon, and reference to Mr. Musk’s goal to “change mankind and make us a multi-planetary species.”

In Anthropic’s promotional video, Dr. Amodei, sporting a teal sweater that went with the earthy colors of his office backdrop, warns within the first few minutes of the potential of artificial intelligence to “make a bioweapon or do a cyberattack.” (Dr. Amodei did call artificial intelligence “the most promising technology in human history” and closed the video by saying he thought A.I. would help end cancer and mental illness within a decade.)

For SpaceX’s I.P.O., which at the time was the largest on record, banks erected rocket ships in their lobbies and served space-themed food in their cafeterias to mark the first day of trading. During Friday’s roadshow event at JPMorgan, the bank handed out leather laptop cases and cookies that simply said “Anthropic.”

Some invisible Wall Street forces are working in Anthropic’s favor.

Because of its sizable valuation and new rules allowing large I.P.O.s to enter major stock indexes more quickly, the company will benefit from billions of dollars from passive index funds and exchange-traded funds that will automatically buy its shares in its early weeks of trading. That creates a can’t-miss feeling among investors who actively manage money and want to keep pace with the broader market.

Until now, Anthropic’s growth has also seeped into investors’ stock portfolios in more indirect ways. The A.I. company’s announcements have at times sent software stocks tumbling, for instance.

“It’s a must own because it’s a hedge against your existing portfolio,” said Jeremy Abelson, founder of Irving Investors, which buys private and public tech stocks.

Dr. Amodei isn’t a brand-new face for many large tech investors. The company raised more than $140 billion privately, including from some of the largest mutual funds, pension funds and sovereign wealth funds, much of it just this year.

Michael Paulus, founder of PCM Encore, a wealth management firm, compared the Anthropic I.P.O. to a promising early-stage start-up investment, on a much a grander scale.

“In the next 10 years, will Anthropic at some point trade down 70 percent, probably?” he said. “Could it be worth 10 times what it’s worth today? It’s also probably true.”

On Tuesday, Morgan Stanley hosted a meeting for investors with Anthropic’s chief financial officer, Krishna Rao. Next week, Mr. Rao and Daniela Amodei, Anthropic’s president and Mr. Amodei’s sister, will meet with investors at Goldman Sachs.

After his talk with Mr. Dimon on Friday, Mary Erdoes, who leads the bank’s asset and wealth management business, reiterated to the room what she deemed a key part of Dr. Amodei’s message.

“The goal is to under promise and to over deliver,” Ms. Erdoes said. “And we sure hope you do that.”

item.title: This Man Stole $9 Million in Gold Bars on the Upper West Side, Police Say
item.description:
The meeting point had been arranged: near 81st Street and Broadway on the Upper West Side.

It was there, in broad daylight, that two men approached each other on a Wednesday in April 2025. One of the men, a 67-year-old New Yorker, transported a bag of $9 million in gold bars, each one the size of a chocolate bar, that the police said someone online had instructed him to buy and hand over.

The man did exactly as he was told, believing that he could secure his financial assets, which an alert on his computer had led to believe were compromised, the authorities said.

The other man took sack of gold and fled on foot, according to the police. The first man had been the victim of an online fraud.

Now, more than a year and a half after the deceit, the New York Police Department is asking for the public’s help in identifying the man who ran off with the gold bars in connection with a grand larceny investigation.

Investigators this week released security camera footage and images of the man suspected of taking the bars.

Isaac Kahan, the owner of Bullion Trading LLC, a gold and silver dealer in Manhattan’s Diamond District, wondered about the sheer logistics that were involved in the heist.

Each of the gold bars weighs one kilogram, about 2.2 pounds, according to the police. While the dollar value of gold has fluctuated since 2025, the current cost of a one-kilo bar is about $130,000, according to Mr. Kahan, meaning that $9 million would buy about 69 gold bars and weigh more than 150 pounds.

“I don’t even know how he would be able to carry that,” Mr. Kahan said in an interview on Friday. “You can’t even lift that.”

From his decades as a precious metals wholesaler, Mr. Kahan said, he had become all too familiar with such fraud schemes, which he noted typically target people in their 70s and 80s, and seek to get them to liquidate their assets to buy gold.

About once every two weeks, Mr. Kahan’s business will receive somewhat cryptic requests from potential clients to buy gold bars, he said, adding that it used to happen on a daily basis. Unlike investors, victims of frauds show little interest in the weight and purity of gold, he said.

“When a person starts throwing the dollar amount first to me, that’s a telltale sign right away,” Mr. Kahan said.

A few years ago, while his company was closed for the Jewish High Holy Days of Rosh Hashana and Yom Kippur, it received several online orders from people who had been targets of such schemes, he said. The business was able to cancel some of the transactions, according to Mr. Kahan, who said one victim’s daughter had contacted him after noticing a suspicious wire transfer for $150,000.

“It was heartbreaking,” Mr. Kahan said, adding that gold is essentially “impossible” to trace.

An older woman in Florida was the target of a similar scheme this May, according to the F.B.I., which said the victim received an email claiming to be from Amazon and telling her to call a phone number because her bank account had been breached.

A person claiming to be associated with the bank told the woman that her identity had been stolen and that her Social Security number had been compromised, which would require her to speak with another individual, who claimed to be an agent with the Federal Trade Commission.

That individual instructed the woman to write a check for $101,220 to buy 21 gold bars that she delivered to a masked man in a Volvo at a Sunoco gas station near the victim’s home in McIntosh, Fla., the authorities said.

When the woman received directions to buy another $500,000 in gold bars, a friend became suspicious, according to federal authorities, who began an investigation and this month announced the indictments of 10 people in connection with the fraud scheme.

It was not clear if there was any connection between the cases in Florida and New York.

The F.B.I. field office in New York did not respond to a request for comment on Friday about the gold bars that were stolen from the man on the Upper West Side.

Mr. Kahan said that he flags suspicious gold purchases for the F.B.I. and arranges for agents to speak to people who he fears could be the targets of frauds.

“We do try to slow the process down,” he said.

item.title: How Some Flights Were Exempt From the Ground Stop
item.description:
Thousands of passengers scrambled to update their travel plans on Saturday as air traffic slowly unsnarled after a nationwide ground stop on Friday, but a number of travelers had already arrived at their destinations on flights left unaffected by the order.

Dozens of international flights took to the skies even as airports across the United States coped with only the third nationwide ground stop issued by the Federal Aviation Administration this century. Certain flights were also permitted to depart from the West Coast to Hawaii during the stoppage.

Here’s why some air travel was allowed to proceed even as flight systems were hampered.

More than 8,200 flights were canceled nationwide on Friday — over 31 percent of those scheduled — according to Cirium, an aviation data firm.

But more than 60 flights bound for overseas left the United States during the stoppage, according to Flightradar24, an aviation tracking site.

There are 21 air traffic control facilities, 20 in the contiguous United States and one in Alaska, that oversee swaths of regions throughout the country, according to the F.A.A.

As some of those centers recovered, flights were “allowed to depart through coordination with the Air Traffic Control System Command Center,” the F.A.A. said in an advisory less than two hours after the ground stop was ordered.

Flights departing for Europe from the Midwest or the East Coast can communicate with the Canadian authorities, said Dan Bubb, a former commercial pilot and an aviation history professor at the University of Las Vegas, Nevada.

Additionally, air traffic over the open ocean is less congested compared with that of the contiguous United States, he said.

Nick Daniels, the president of the National Air Traffic Controllers Association, said that for planes traveling such a large distance over oceanic airspace, “they have process procedures, different standards of separations, than what we do to run the volume of air traffic” in the lower 48 states.

At 3 p.m. Pacific Standard Time on Friday, about two hours before the nationwide ground stop was lifted, San Francisco International Airport said that Pacific-bound flights, including to Hawaii and Asia, had been cleared for departure.

Why were passengers flying west so fortunate?

Those pilots generally will talk to one of the regional centers until reaching cruising altitude, Dr. Bubb said.

Centers handling air traffic headed to Hawaii or Asia are outside the contiguous United States, and therefore could avoid long delays from the ground stop, he said. At a certain altitude, a pilot could swap communications with California controllers for those in Hawaii or Alaska, he added.

Flights within Alaska, those from the West Coast to Hawaii and international flights from Honolulu were also exempt from the ground stop, Alaska Airlines said in statement.

Areas like Alaska, Guam and Hawaii are far enough removed that they can remain stable even as systems are affected in the contiguous United States, Mr. Daniels said.

“If they would have seen any kind of risk in the system there as well, then they would have reacted the same to reduce the capacity,” he added.

Generally, yes.

During ground stops and delays, emergency and medical aircraft are given clearance to take off.

Life Flight Network, a medical transport service, said in a social media post on Friday that “EMS aircraft are exempt from this restriction,” and its services were operating normally.

“Above all is medevac and law enforcement,” Mr. Daniels said. “They get a priority movement throughout the system, and we move other aircraft out of their way, versus, they need to get in line with everyone else.”

Pilots and controllers have many tools to communicate, Dr. Bubb said.

Pilots can talk to one another, their companies and ground control through different messaging systems even if one fails.

“There are redundant systems where pilots can talk to each other, and we can sequence ourselves, but we follow the instructions that we were given by air traffic control,” Dr. Bubb said.

item.title: She Was a CBS News Producer When Few Women Were
item.description:
Linda Mason, an Emmy Award-winning journalist at CBS News who was the first female producer at “CBS Evening News” with Walter Cronkite and who was put in charge of reinforcing the division’s standards after a botched “60 Minutes” report on President George W. Bush’s military service, died on Oct. 28 at her home in the Bronx. She was 84.

Her husband, Cary Aminoff, said the cause was dementia.

Ms. Mason stood out for her long rise through the male-dominated news division. She started as a desk assistant at CBS Radio before moving into jobs of increasing responsibility, including senior producer of “CBS Evening News”; executive producer of “CBS News Sunday Morning” and the documentary news series “CBS Reports”; and vice president of public affairs, developing programming and overseeing standards.

She was also known as a mentor to other women at the network.

“We took it for granted that every woman was going to be a secretary or a researcher, and she had made it to the exalted position of producer,” Marcy McGinnis, who started at CBS News as a secretary and later became a producer and senior vice president of news coverage, said in an interview. “I looked to her as my North Star. Oh, I wanted to be like her. And she was nice to me and other people like me who didn’t matter at the time.”

In 2004, as a vice president, Ms. Mason was CBS News’s liaison to an independent review panel convened by the network to investigate a flawed “60 Minutes Wednesday” report about Mr. Bush, which was broadcast two months before his successful campaign for re-election. It purported to raise serious questions about the president’s Vietnam-era Texas Air National Guard service and whether he had received preferential treatment because of his family’s political connections.

Her role was to answer questions from the panel — led by Louis D. Boccardi, a former chief executive of The Associated Press, and Dick Thornburgh, a former attorney general of the United States — about CBS’s reporting methods.

“For months, I felt as if I were in isolation, quarantined,” she wrote in her memoir, “Speak Up: Breaking the Glass Ceiling at CBS News” (2023). “It was a very difficult time for me since I was used to being involved in all the events CBS was covering and talking with my colleagues.”

The panel concluded that the report had used documents said to be from Mr. Bush’s commander but that they had not been authenticated, that inattentive executives had approved it without rudimentary fact-checking and that it had been anchored by an overworked Dan Rather, who was also the anchor of “CBS Evening News.” He had left the scene of Hurricane Frances in Florida to do an interview for the report.

CBS fired its producer, Mary Mapes, and demanded the resignations of three executives who had overseen the segment.

After the panel’s report was released, Ms. Mason told “PBS NewsHour” that the episode was “very embarrassing to those of us at CBS News.” She added, “It’s going to serve to raise the consciousness of everybody here on how we have to do things better.”

Ms. Mason was promoted to senior vice president of standards and special projects. In that role, she oversaw the news division’s adherence to its existing rules of ethics and journalism and added new ones to prohibit political contributions and require approval for outside writing.

Her job also included reviewing investigative programming and potentially sensitive news segments; approving segments using hidden cameras; overseeing the use of confidential sources; and helping determine the reliability of documents.

“Linda was the conscience of CBS News,” Sean McManus, the president of CBS News from 2005 to 2011, said in an interview. “If there was a question in the division about standards or what was appropriate, Linda was the last wall of defense.”

Linda Sue Mason was born on Feb. 26, 1942, in Middletown, N.Y., about 70 miles northwest of Manhattan. Her father, Harry Mason, was a dentist, and her mother, Betty (Sanders) Mason, was a schoolteacher. When Linda was 8, polio caused partial paralysis on her right side; she recovered, but her right fingers were no longer flexible, which made it difficult to type later in her life.

At Pembroke College, the women’s school at Brown University, she was a freelance reporter at The Providence Journal. She briefly continued at the paper full-time after graduating with a bachelor’s degree in international relations in 1964. A year later, she received a master’s degree in filmmaking from Syracuse University, where she learned skills she would need for a career in TV journalism.

Ms. Mason joined CBS Radio in 1966. After two years, she was hired as a writer at “CBS Morning News,” where she produced reports but did not have a producer title. The show’s executive producer was stunned when she asked for a promotion in 1971.

In her memoir, she recalled him telling her, “Women can’t be producers.” She told him, “But I have been producing reports for two years.”

He promoted her several months later after he was promoted as well. Later that year, she was hired as a producer at “CBS Evening News,” the highest-rated network news broadcast. She eventually became a senior producer, staying at the flagship broadcast through 1986, five years into Mr. Rather’s tenure as Mr. Cronkite’s successor.

“She was supremely intelligent,” said Andrew Heyward, a producer who worked for her at “CBS Evening News” and was president of CBS News from 1996 to 2005. “At a time when the culture was not only male but put a huge premium on clubbability, she wasn’t clubby but so smart that she was a force to be reckoned with.”

For “CBS Evening News,” her work included reporting from Afghanistan and Vietnam as well as Beijing during the 1989 pro-democracy uprising in Tiananmen Square.

She was also a producer of “The Trouble With Rock,” a 1974 investigative documentary about the influence of the Mafia, drugs and payola in the music industry, including CBS Records, which the report accused of giving money and heroin and other drugs to disc jockeys in return for air play at radio stations.

“Without question,” Ms. Mason wrote in her book, “this delicate project taught me how to walk a tightrope when looking inside my own company.”

She won 13 Emmys and three Peabody Awards during her career.

Ms. Mason, who retired in 2013, is survived by her husband of 56 years; a daughter, Elissa Aminoff; a sister, Nancy Hauser; a brother, Roger; and a grandson. Another daughter, Beth Aminoff, died last year.

In 2000, Ms. Mason wrote a report for CBS on what had gone wrong after hers and other networks projected and then retracted that the Democratic nominee, Vice President Al Gore, was the winner of Florida’s electoral votes in the presidential election that year. In the disputed vote recount that followed, there was much legal wrangling by the nominees before the U.S. Supreme Court ruled against further recounts and effectively gave the state’s electoral votes — and the election — to Mr. Bush.

Four years later, Ms. Mason was put in charge of the network’s election night coverage. “We’d rather be last and right than first and wrong,” she told The Baltimore Sun the day before the election.

item.title: Family Dollar to Pay $63 Million Settlement for Overcharging Customers
item.description:
Family Dollar has agreed to pay a $63 million settlement after federal and state authorities filed complaints against the company for charging customers more than amounts advertised in mailers and displayed on store shelves.

The settlement, which was announced by the Federal Trade Commission on Thursday, came alongside a same-day order, filed in the U.S. District Court for the Eastern District of Virginia.

The order seeks to prevent the retailer from continuing its deceptive pricing practices and would require it to create a “pricing accuracy program,” to be independently certified on an annual basis.

“Today’s order will ensure Family Dollar stops deceiving consumers about its prices and returns money to consumers harmed by these practices,” Christopher Mufarrige, the director of the F.T.C.’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in the announcement.

The agreement is the result of a complaint filed by the commission and 17 states on Thursday, which claimed that Family Dollar had overcharged consumers “millions of dollars” since January 2023.

The F.T.C. and Family Dollar did not immediately respond to requests for comment on Saturday. In the order, Family Dollar said that it neither admitted to nor denied any of the allegations in the complaint.

The complaint highlighted a number of cases in which customers, attracted to deals advertised digitally and in circulars, had visited their local Family Dollar store, only to be charged a higher price at checkout.

One individual in Columbus, Ohio, filed a complaint in July 2023 with the Better Business Bureau about a cereal deal that promised that the second box would cost only $1. Once at the store, the cashier “did not honor it,” the customer said, claiming that she “was not aware of such a sale.”

Another customer, in Michigan, reported in January 2025 that a store would not honor a two for $20 deal for packs of Pampers diapers, despite a discount label displayed on the store shelf, according to the complaint.

The manager “quickly removed the shelf tags,” the customer said, “and told me that the price will not be honored.”

Shoppers at Family Dollar stores in several states reported similar experiences with the Pampers two for $20 deal, according to the complaint.

“This pattern is documented across numerous state audits, consumer complaints and F.T.C. undercover purchases,” the complaint said.

Eggs, milk, cleaning supplies, laundry detergent, toilet paper, iced tea and coffee were also among the many household items noted in the complaint.

A $3.55 half-gallon of milk in Pennsylvania became $4.15 at checkout. A roll of 16 Energizer AA batteries advertised at $11.50 was rung up for $13.50 in Ohio. A bedsheet set labeled $10 in Florida was charged as $12.

Family Dollar, which was founded in 1959, has 7,000 locations across the United States and prides itself on its low, family-friendly prices, with most of its products selling for under $5.

Many customers live on “razor-thin margins,” according to the complaint, and even slight increases in price “can lead to real, adverse consequences.”

“Despite widespread consumer complaints and increasing regulatory scrutiny, Family Dollar has failed to implement adequate safeguards to prevent continued overcharging,” it added.

The $63 million settlement calls for a $40 million fund to distribute payments to customers, as well as $20 million worth of discounts, to be rolled out as a 15 percent price reduction on most items for at least two consecutive days, according to the order.

The remaining $3 million will be distributed to the 17 state plaintiffs, the order notes.

On Oct. 26, the F.T.C. and 20 states filed similar charges against another discount retailer, Dollar General.

From Jan. 1, 2019, through March 31, 2026, according to that complaint, Dollar General exhibited “pervasive and systemic pricing inaccuracies” that involved charging prices higher than advertised and displayed on labels in stores.

The retailer, which operates more than 20,000 stores nationwide, bills itself as “America’s neighborhood general store.”

Dollar General did not immediately respond to a request for comment on Saturday.

item.title: SpaceX Makes History With Successful Rocket Catch in Texas
item.description:
SpaceX’s giant Starship spacecraft pulled off a remarkable feat on Saturday afternoon in the quest to build fully reusable rockets. For the first time, the spacecraft successfully returned from orbit to its launch site in South Texas, where it was caught between two mechanical arms on the launch tower.

For the past decade, SpaceX has successfully landed the boosters of its smaller Falcon 9 rockets and then reused them on subsequent launches. But the upper stages of the Falcon 9s are still thrown away each time.

The Starship rocket system is not only much larger than Falcon 9, but it was designed from the start to be fully reusable. Bringing back an upper stage from orbit is a major technical hurdle, and SpaceX was able to pull it off on its first try.

Jared Isaacman, the NASA administrator, offered his congratulations on X. “Making more believers by the day….one step closer to,” he wrote, adding an emoji of the moon and the American flag. Starship is slated to serve as one of two lander designs that will take astronauts to the surface of the moon as part of NASA’s Artemis program.

Elon Musk, the chief executive of SpaceX, posted a video on X showing a view of Starship from below, part of the post-landing inspection.

A few hours earlier, the spacecraft, which is about 170 feet long, had been traveling at more than 17,000 miles per hour at an altitude of 170 miles. Then, one of its engines fired briefly, nudging it out of orbit to begin its fall back to Earth.

As Starship entered the atmosphere, the pressure and friction of air heated the belly of the spacecraft and slowed its velocity. When it reached the denser parts of the atmosphere, flaps at the front and back steered it as it passed over Mexico before returning to Starbase, SpaceX’s facility at the southern tip of Texas.

With the final landing burn, Starship pivoted to a vertical position, hovered and then slid between the mechanical arms that gently closed around it.

This was the 15th test flight of Starship, a mission that began when it launched on Friday afternoon. It was not a complete success. The bottom booster stage, known as Super Heavy, accomplished its main objective of pushing the upper-stage spacecraft through the densest part of the atmosphere and then dropped away.

SpaceX had hoped that it would be able to catch Super Heavy at the launchpad, much as it did with the upper stage on Saturday.

But as the booster headed back, it detected a problem and instead performed a simulated landing over the Gulf of Mexico. SpaceX is still investigating what happened.

The Starship spacecraft continued to orbit and deployed 26 of the company’s next-generation Starlink satellites.

The words “DON’T PANIC” were printed on the side of the spacecraft, a reference to Douglas Adams’s “The Hitchhiker’s Guide to the Galaxy.” This particular ship was No. 42 off the production line, and in Mr. Adams’s book, 42 was the answer to the ultimate question of life, the universe and everything.

After about 22 hours and 14 orbits, Starship then returned to Earth.

Unlike Friday, when the skies over Starbase were cloudless and filled with sunshine, Saturday was cool, breezy and gray. In the final seconds, the spacecraft dropped through the clouds, and its engines fired one more time to pivot to vertical, hover and slide between the chopstick arms.

Now that Flight 15 has ended with a successful catch in Texas, Flight 16 could be the first Starship launch from SpaceX’s revamped launchpad at the Kennedy Space Center in Florida. The Starbase launch site is not sufficient to serve SpaceX’s planned acceleration of Starship launches. Another Florida launchpad is under construction at the Cape Canaveral Space Force Station, and SpaceX has announced plans to build a huge launch complex in Louisiana.

SpaceX could also hit a major milestone next year if it can launch two Starships in quick succession, dock them together in orbit and then move liquid methane and liquid oxygen propellants from one Starship to the other.

This refueling maneuver is essential for Starship to leave low-Earth orbit. Without it, the spacecraft could not make it to the moon for NASA, or head to more distant destinations like Mars, where Mr. Musk hopes to send people someday.

SpaceX’s Starship is also slated to participate in its first NASA mission in the second half of next year. That flight, known as Artemis III, will stay in low-Earth orbit, where Starship will practice docking with NASA’s Orion crew capsule.

In the original mission design, Starship and Orion were to travel separately to lunar orbit and dock there. But SpaceX wants the two spacecraft to dock in low-Earth orbit and then have Starship provide the propulsion to get them to the moon.

item.title: In a Sloppified A.I. World, Only Humans Can Build ‘Ecosystems’
item.description:
Networking has long been crucial in tech, an industry where so-called warm intros, founder dinners and alumni communities are central to the culture (and to deal making).

But lately, start-ups and venture capital firms have been sharpening their focus on human connection, by hiring people for “ecosystem” jobs. Such roles, which have titles like “start-up ecosystem lead” or “ecosystem growth manager,” focus on building or maintaining relationships among various parties on a company’s behalf. In this way, the people ushering in the artificial intelligence revolution are doubling down on in-person ties.

The workers in such roles often spend their days planning events, orchestrating partnerships, supporting clients and leading trainings. Are the tasks new? Not really. But the framing is.

“When companies talk about ecosystem, they are talking about trying to cultivate and tend to an extended network — not just of customers but also of partners, distribution channels, supporters and advocates,” said Yoni Rechtman, a partner at Slow Ventures, a venture capital firm.

The venture capital firm Andreessen Horowitz defined ecosystem as “the bottom-up vector of trust in venture,” and the firm’s “ecosystem lead” explained his role as “focused on expanding and reinforcing the multitude of networks spanning our firm.”

Ecosystem roles exist on various teams, including marketing, partnerships and sales, and the job’s specifics vary from company to company, said Natalie Sportelli, who since January has held the title “start-up ecosystem” at Clay, an A.I. sales tool start-up. In recent months, her projects have included putting together product demonstrations for a partner’s portfolio companies, coordinating product coaching sessions with customers and collaborating with other start-up program leaders for a panel in London about building A.I.-native sales organizations.

“We’re not just trying to sell — we’re trying to create programming that makes start-ups successful,” she said.

Though the role is still niche, the rate of job titles with “ecosystem” in them quadrupled on LinkedIn from 2010 to 2025, according to Nick Bloom and Gideon Slocum Moore, researchers at Stanford who have analyzed job-title data on the platform. (Only a small share of new “ecosystem” roles in recent years, they noted, appear related to the field of ecology.)

People in tech have dropped the phrase ecosystem for as long as Mr. Rechtman can remember — referring to the “tech ecosystem” and the “start-up ecosystem” — but its presence in job titles is a more recent development, he said. Ms. Sportelli, too, has noticed an uptick in such roles in the past year, which she attributes partly to a hunger for connection brought on by the rise of A.I. Lately, there is a “premium on in-person,” including events, she said.

The bet is that people beget interest from other people.

“It’s very difficult to stand out in a sloppified feed and a sloppified inbox,” Mr. Rechtman said, referring to A.I. slop. In a world where companies can easily blast potential customers with A.I.-generated content all day, he added, “getting attention is much harder, and you need to be more creative in how you meet people and build relationships with them.”

A wave of new A.I. tools also means a wave of new stakeholders and relationships to manage.

“People now have a ton of vendors, and those vendors all need to work together — and the relationships between them are more complicated,” Mr. Rechtman said.

The A.I. era has spawned a number of new job functions — with trendy new titles to go with them.

“There are some roles that come into vogue because they sound cool or because you feel like you’re investing in the right things by hiring for them,” Ms. Sportelli said. “Start-up and venture people love a good branding moment when it comes to job titles.”

item.title: Behind the All-American Ralph Lauren Brand Is a French C.E.O.
item.description:
Ralph Lauren is going through a renaissance.

But when Patrice Louvet took over as chief executive in 2017, the company was at a low point. His predecessor, the first chief of the firm not named Ralph Lauren, stepped down after a little more than a year amid creative clashes with the eponymous founder.

Mr. Louvet, 62, was an unexpected choice. Born in France, he served in the French Navy and spent nearly 30 years at Procter & Gamble, known for selling razors and shampoo, not polo shirts and knit sweaters.

Under his leadership, the brand started relying less on heavy discounting and pulled out of lower-tier stores. Its preppy look is once again popular with young people. Reservations are essential at its packed restaurants, and at the coffee shops, the lines are long. The company’s share price has risen more than 400 percent since Mr. Louvet took the top job.

Last fiscal year, Ralph Lauren brought in $8.1 billion in revenue, a 14 percent increase. It recently raised its forecast for sales and profit margins for the current year, ahead of the holiday shopping season.

Like other retailers, Ralph Lauren must try to remain relevant as trends shift rapidly and politics increasingly intrudes on culture. The company has many stakeholders, but the Lauren family controls more than 80 percent of the vote among shareholders.

Mr. Louvet has picked up many lessons from Mr. Lauren, 87, who is chief creative officer and executive chairman, that have helped guide him on where to take the brand next.

“In this industry, if all you do is magic, then you can build a nice little business, but it’s not going to go very far,” Mr. Louvet said. “If all you do is logic, you can’t be successful in this industry.” Success, he says, is striking a balance between the two.

This interview has been edited and condensed.

People want to know the relationship that you have with Ralph Lauren, the man. How do you work together?

One of the key reasons I left Procter & Gamble is the opportunity to work with Ralph. There are very few visionary philanthropists, entrepreneurs, innovators like him.

We took a lot of time to understand each other as humans, not as businesspeople, before we both signed in May 2017.

We never documented what our respective roles were.

All the McKinsey people right now are lifting their heads and saying, “What?”

Yeah, exactly. No job description. Instinctively, intuitively, we got clear on our respective lanes.

Ralph is very focused on the creative vision of the company. I focus on just running the company and delivering for the near term and the long term.

How has the relationship changed?

The nature of the relationship with Ralph hasn’t changed dramatically. If anything, we’ve become really close friends. We have lunch together every week when we’re not traveling. We might spend two, three hours together and not a minute on business.

The trust has been built over time. There’s been very few situations where we weren’t aligned from the get-go on specific decisions, which is pretty unique 10 years in.

Ralph talks about magic and gut instinct, and you come from an operational background focused on logic and spreadsheets. What’s an example of when you two differed on a business decision?

We did a beautiful fashion show and the theme was “Ralph’s Club.” Janelle Monáe was there, she sang and she got on the tables. It was spectacular. Black tie. After that, Ralph said: “Let’s open a club. I love that spirit, that atmosphere. Magic.”

But the financials made no sense. Ralph, as he often is, was very passionate about it. We ultimately decided this is when the logic needs to override the magic.

The American flag has always played a role in the Ralph Lauren brand. How do you protect what feels essential about the brand while also not having it be politicized?

This company has been around for 60 years. We focus on values that ultimately are universal values, not political values: optimism, authenticity, quality, entrepreneurship, family. The brand is resonating so well in Sydney, in Shanghai, in Chicago, because these values resonate with everyone around the world.

Our business internationally is actually even stronger than it is in the U.S. China is up 35 percent. We’ve been growing north of 20 percent for several years, at a time where the geopolitical situation is tense between those two markets. This is true across every market.

Is it possible to bring clothing production to the United States?

We are keen to bring production to the U.S. We manufacture all our Olympic gear here, as we get ready for the L.A. 2028 Olympics, which will be a big moment for our company. We manufacture a number of our luxury products here. There’s a manufacturing site in Queens.

Our products are pretty sophisticated. I don’t think we want to necessarily drive massive T-shirt manufacturing in the U.S. But certainly the intent is there, the interest is there.

Trend-wise, Ralph is back. But what happens if the fashion cycle changes?

Ralph has many wonderful quotes, including this one: “I don’t want to be too hot and I don’t want to be too cold.” We’re not looking to chase trends.

The majority of our business — more than 70 percent — is our core products that are available year in, year out. We might evolve the color, we might evolve the sizing. It might be a bit oversized or it might be slim fit. But that tweed jacket, that white polo shirt, that rugby shirt, that cable knit sweater, those are staples that stay all year and across time.

One of the pivots we made when we started this journey 10 years ago is to be much more consumer centric. The younger generation was on TikTok. We couldn’t spell TikTok. They were shopping on e-commerce platforms. We weren’t there. They were gaming. We weren’t there.

And we said, “If we want to talk to that young generation and bring them in, let’s understand where they want to engage with brands, where they want to shop, and let’s make sure we’re there in a way that’s consistent with our brand image.”

Many young people are finding the brand through the secondary market. Some brands see the secondhand clothing market as diluting a brand. But your company recently hosted PoloFest, an event selling vintage Ralph clothes, in Tokyo.

Ralph has always been about timelessness. The vision is for products to be handed down, for the father to hand it to his son, for grandmother to hand to the granddaughter.

A lot of people discover our brand, particularly the younger generation now, through secondary markets, which is pretty neat. They become part of that ecosystem, and then ultimately come to our store at full price. You will see a lot of vintage in our stores.

Tell me about your upbringing. You were born in France.

I was born in a little town called Saint-Cloud, just outside Paris. My father was an engineer and worked for a French chemical company. My mother was a homemaker and she did philanthropic activities. I’m the eldest of four.

What was a formative time in your childhood?

When I was 9, my father was sent to New Jersey. I was not particularly excited to leave my friends, my school, my activities, my environment. I was thrown into American public school, not speaking any English. The first few months were rough.

My father had studied at M.I.T., so he knew a little bit of the U.S., but my three siblings, my mom and I were all discovering the U.S. at the same time. I think there’s strength in everyone going through the same experience.

You spent nearly 30 years at P&G. I read that an employee once told you that you were not the right leader. How did that affect you?

It was a massive gut punch. I was in charge of hair care and health care in Japan and Korea, my first general manager role. I am sent there with a very clear mission: to turn the business around. I came in all guns blazing with a sense of urgency.

I learned you must clarify the direction and the vision. It was clear in my head, but I had not really democratized it. Define it overtly and then make sure you’re engaging everyone around it. Don’t move before you’ve done that.

It’s time for the lightning round. What do you wear to feel most confident?

What you’re seeing today. A blue pinstriped suit. Ralph Lauren watch — also available in women’s.

What’s one fashion trend you cannot stand?

White socks and slides.

What are you personally trying to learn right now?

Artificial intelligence, particularly agents.

What’s the last question you asked A.I.?

I asked it last night, what were the drivers to the stock price decline after earnings.

How do you sign off to your emails?

Onwards and upwards, together.

What’s one place that you think people should still be wearing ties but aren’t?

We should be wearing ties everywhere.

Tell me about an object in your office and the significance of it.

Someone from my team gave me a little Yoda. This is an industry where there’s a lot of emotion. There’s a good amount of intensity. Yoda is a good reminder to just breathe and don’t overreact.

item.title: A Human Reads the Anthropic I.P.O. Filing
item.description:
My breath taken, I looked up from my desk to gaze at the red-orange blanket of fallen leaves just outside my window. I needed the pause, or maybe the distraction, from what I was reading.

The thick document before me looked like any other standard business proposal: a prospectus for an initial public offering with boilerplate language about dividends, compensation and Class A stock. But the more I read, the more it morphed into experimental literature, equal parts business plan, philosophical treatise and sci-fi thriller.

This will be an I.P.O. unlike any other, its language both matter-of-fact and unnerving, its ultimate subject our future. Not futures, as in the stock market, but the future, as in what it might look like and whether we have one.

The prospectus comes from Anthropic, the artificial intelligence concern immersed in the technologies rapidly transforming the human experience. It is poised to offer shares to the public for the first time, and this document, recently filed with the Securities and Exchange Commission, lays out its blueprint for potential investors to decide whether to bet on the future of civilization.

I cannot give you odds on this existential gamble. My prior awareness of Anthropic extended little beyond clicking on a button with hundreds of thousands of other writers to join a massive class-action copyright lawsuit. As someone who knows next to nothing about investments, I read the Anthropic prospectus solely out of my vested interest as a human being.

In seeking the considerable capital needed for chips, data centers and electricity, the company — with an estimated valuation well north of $1 trillion — begins its pitch by dangling the possibility that artificial intelligence could “solve problems that have resisted generations of human effort.”

It asks us to imagine its A.I. models as “a country of geniuses in a data center,” working in concert to improve our quality of life. Helping to cure disease. Connecting the underserved to medical expertise. Increasing economic productivity. Improving government services. (In California, it says, Anthropic’s chatbot, Claude, is already “helping to shorten the lines at the DMV.”)

You’d have to be a robot not to … Let me rephrase: You’d have to be a toaster oven not to want an end to both cancer and the long lines at the DMV.

Anthropic is a public benefit corporation, dedicated to balancing social responsibility with profit, and its seven co-founders have championed a measured approach to developing what the prospectus calls “the most transformative technology in human history.” It advocates for developers to compete over safety and security, “rather than rushing to release increasingly powerful models without adequate safeguards.”

In discussing a particularly advanced form of A.I. that Anthropic expects to match or surpass human capability and become widely available, the document says: “If Powerful A.I. is directed at solving humanity’s hardest problems and the risks are managed responsibly, the potential is extraordinary.”

If.

If we work together to ensure the safe and responsible growth of machine intelligence, the prospectus seems to be saying, what a wonderful world this will be (notwithstanding an economic disruption “greater in magnitude” than any other technical advancement in history). If not, then economic upheaval may be the least of our worries.

Keep in mind, dear potential investor: “To build A.I. is to harness cognition itself, and anything so powerful can be used for ill as well as good.”

The foreboding I began to feel intensified the more I read. Throughout the document’s 300-plus pages are hair-on-fire sentences delivered in the flat language of business. Sentences such as:

“A.I. can be misused by those who wish to do harm, for example to conduct cyberattacks or to design biological weapons.”

And:

“Authoritarian governments may use A.I. to create high-tech surveillance states, deepen repression, and make themselves much more difficult to dislodge.”

Even more unsettling is the acknowledged risk of artificial intelligence becoming so autonomous that humans might lose control: “Our A.I. models may behave in unintended, misaligned, or autonomous ways, including by taking harmful actions that no user or third party directed.”

It is one thing to recall similar cautions from the astrophysicist Stephen Hawking in a 2014 interview; quite another to read these warnings amid discussions of income tax implications.

At times, the prospectus evokes a muffled Mayday call struggling to convey calm. Consider this mouthful of a paragraph:

“Concerns have been raised both within our organization and by other researchers, regulators, policymakers, and industry participants that sufficiently advanced A.I. systems could, if not developed, deployed, and operated with appropriate safeguards, oversight, and security measures, pose catastrophic or existential risks to humanity, particularly if such systems were misused, replicated, weaponized, or allowed to operate with a high degree of autonomy.”

Catastrophic or existential risks to humanity?

To Anthropic’s credit, it dedicates more than a quarter of its prospectus — 93 pages — to “risk factors,” a rare, perhaps unprecedented, transparency about the potential downsides of a business proposal. Imagine, for example, if Facebook’s initial public offering in 2012 had, in addition to boasting of a more open and connected world, addressed the mental health impact on children.

Anthropic does not understate the magnitude of the risks it lays out. Perhaps there was no way to mention only in passing the potential for the end to life as we know it.

Last year the company’s chief executive officer, Dario Amodei, put the odds of A.I. leading to the end of civilization at between 10 and 25 percent. He has since downplayed the doomsday scenario, arguing in part that the odds drop if governments and the tech industry commit to a more deliberate, safety-first approach to A.I. development.

Beyond its conjuring of a new and better world, the Anthropic prospectus is, in the end, an investment proposal in which Dr. Amodei and his co-founders each have a stake worth an estimated $18 billion. Such outsize numbers only intensify the sense that a chosen few humans — fallible, like all humans — will decide what comes next, leaving the rest of us to hold our collective breath.

I came away from reading the Anthropic prospectus with no desire to get in on the ground floor of a never-before-seen opportunity, no matter how transparent the pitch. I didn’t want in on this cosmic bet.

Instead, I got up from the desk and took my dog for a long walk through another Technicolor autumn day, so familiar and, suddenly, so precious.

item.title: Tears and Disbelief in Taiwan, Where Jensen Huang Is a Celebrity
item.description:
When the news broke in Taiwan on Thursday night that Jensen Huang had resigned as Nvidia’s chief executive, Ray Wang was too upset to sleep. He drank a whole bottle of red wine and prayed for Mr. Huang.

A hairstylist, Mr. Wang, has been cutting Mr. Huang’s hair, watching it change from salt-and-pepper to silver, for nearly a decade.

“Maybe they’ll bring him back,” Mr. Wang said, “the way Apple brought back Steve Jobs.”

Mr. Huang has many well-wishers like this in Taiwan. An American citizen, he moved to the United States when he was 9 years old, but he was born on the island and enjoys a godlike status there. Fans mobbed him at night markets and lined up for autographs. Restaurants where he has eaten hang his photo, Hollywood-celebrity style. He has been hailed as the “pride of Taiwan” and affectionately called “the people’s dad.” The frenzy around his visits became known as “Jensanity,” a play on the “Linsanity” that followed Jeremy Lin, the Taiwanese-American professional basketball player.

Mr. Huang co-founded Nvidia in 1993, and it became one of the world’s most valuable companies in recent years by making advanced chips for artificial intelligence. Over the decades, Mr. Huang made Nvidia’s relationship with Taiwan personal.

Taiwan is home to TSMC, the premier semiconductor chip maker that produces roughly 90 percent of the world’s most advanced chips and is the main reason Taiwan’s economy is projected to grow around 12 percent this year. It is Taiwan’s most important company, and Nvidia is TSMC’s biggest customer.

Mr. Huang’s resignation followed reports of affairs, one with an Nvidia executive and another with a businesswoman, Alice Huang, whom U.S. intelligence officials suspected of providing intelligence for China. Beijing has denied the allegation.

His downfall landed with dismay and disbelief in Taiwan, where he had effectively cultivated relationships. Mr. Huang knew the people who made his chips and servers, and he made a point of crediting them in public.

He went to great lengths to show his appreciation for business partners — and get what he wanted. Last November, when he needed TSMC to allocate more production capacity to Nvidia, he flew to Taiwan and sat down for hot pot with its senior executives, Liang-Rong Chen, a tech journalist who was there, told me. He patiently signed whiskey bottles for its employees.

Mr. Chen explained why that mattered. Squeezing more chips out of a busy factory took many managers willing to rearrange production and staff willing to work overtime. Mr. Chen, who writes the newsletter Tech Taiwan, suspected they would not have been as eager to do it for other American tech giants because none of them had gone to the great lengths as Mr. Huang in cultivating relationships.

A longtime semiconductor analyst, who was not authorized to speak publicly, told me that without Nvidia there would be no A.I. as we see it today. Suppliers have grown accustomed to taking their cues from Mr. Huang, he said, who had a sense of where the technology was headed and was able to persuade the companies to go along with him despite the risks at times. With him gone, the analyst wondered whose judgment they would trust.

“We hope things won’t change too much because he understands Taiwan better than anyone.” Chin-Tsang Ho, Taiwan’s deputy minister of economic affairs, told me just hours before Mr. Huang stepped down.

Four days before Mr. Huang’s resignation, TSMC was arranging a call with Mr. Huang to discuss plans for the next few years, said Chun-Hsien Yeh, who heads Taiwan’s National Development Council and sits on TSMC’s board. Mr. Yeh told me he expected Mr. Huang’s resignation would have little impact on TSMC, however. Demand for A.I. chips was already exceeding supply, and other customers, including AMD, needed them, too. “If Nvidia takes less,” he said. “others will take more.”

Quite a few people I talked to, including semiconductor insiders, said they believed that Mr. Huang didn’t deserve the treatment. “We felt the process didn’t seem quite fair,” Da-Xiang Hu, a tech professional in Taipei, told me. “We felt it all happened too fast.”

A few even saw his downfall in conspiratorial terms, imagining that other American business and political leaders grew wary of the growing influence of tech executives of Taiwanese and Chinese descent and worked to push Mr. Huang out.

Other people were annoyed that their Nvidia shares fell. In a place where many people own shares in TSMC, social media quickly filled with joking anxieties about the fate of that company. On Threads, one user posted a photo of TSMC’s chief executive, Che-Chia Wei, captioning it, “Please don’t have an affair. Please. Please.” A commenter responded, “If you do have an affair, please don’t choose a Chinese spy. Please 🙏” Both the post and the comment were liked tens of thousands of times.

Many Taiwanese commentators and social media users are supportive of Mr. Huang. They thanked him for bringing business to the island and for shining a spotlight on its companies.

Emmy Hu, a financial content creator, wrote on Facebook that other tech giants had squeezed Taiwanese suppliers on price. “His generosity toward Taiwan was unusual,” she wrote of Mr. Huang. Yu Ting-hao, a financial commentator, called Mr. Huang “Taiwan’s biggest advocate” on his YouTube program. Kang Wen-teng, who runs a hot pot restaurant in Taichung City, told me he wanted people to remember what Mr. Huang had done for Taiwan. “Thank you, Papa Huang,” he wrote on Threads.

Still, the accusations that Mr. Huang had an affair with a woman suspected of being a Chinese intelligence asset troubled even his fans. Da-Xiang Hu, the tech professional in Taipei, told me how moved she was whenever Mr. Huang spoke about Taiwan abroad. After decades of Chinese pressure that has kept Taiwan isolated internationally, hearing him say “Taiwan” mattered to her. At the same time, she said, she feels uneasy about Mr. Huang’s public push to sell advanced chips to China. In a Threads post in which she thanked him, Ms. Hu wondered whether Nvidia’s chips might someday help a Chinese missile strike Taiwan more precisely. “I wish you well,” she wrote, “and I hope Taiwan stays safe.”

In Taiwan, there is even chatter that maybe Mr. Huang could come back and become the chief executive or a board member of TSMC.

To Mr. Wang, the hairstylist, Mr. Huang was both a visionary entrepreneur and an old friend. He was planning to write to him. “If he comes back to Taiwan,” he said, “I’m sure he’d come in for a haircut.”

item.title: When Tech ‘Upgrades’ Go Awry
item.description:
Planes grounded. Office work ground to a halt.

The past few days have served as a vivid reminder of our deep and mostly unthinking dependence on technology. It’s powerful, it’s ubiquitous and yet, at times, it can be alarmingly fragile.

Old technology and new technology were the culprits. Starting on Thursday, Microsoft’s email, office and meeting software — delivered over the internet — stopped working for millions of users worldwide. Those cloud services were restored on Saturday.

On Friday, the Federal Aviation Administration ordered all flights grounded after some of its aged data-handling equipment faltered, raising potential safety issues. The order was lifted Friday night, but hundreds of thousands of passengers were stranded over the weekend.

A telling irony is that both meltdowns were caused by attempted “upgrades” that went awry. New cables in the case of the F.A.A., and a planned increase in computing capacity in Microsoft’s case.

The upgrade challenge underlines the extraordinary complexity of multilayered combinations of hardware and software in major computing systems. Upset the delicate balance by making changes, even in an effort to improve performance, and you risk a system crash.

That happens frequently, though widespread outages are uncommon. The last big one came two years ago, when what should have been a routine software update by a security company, CrowdStrike, crashed millions of computers around the world that were running Microsoft Windows. Airlines grounded flights. Subways stopped. Operators of 911 lines couldn’t dispatch help. Stores shut down. Hospitals canceled surgeries. It took days to restore all the impaired machines.

One reason for the confounding complexity is that the computing systems used in major industries like banking, health care and transportation have been steadily built up over the years. These systems can be thought of almost as digital versions of geological formations — with changes in hardware and software similar to layers of sediment piling up. New layers are added, but on top of old ones.

An early computer programming language, COBOL, was created in 1959 by a “short-term committee” whose task was to design something suitable for use in business. The programming language was intended to be a place holder until a more polished version was developed.

Jean Sammet, a member of COBOL’s design team, recalled that the group saw their work as a “stop gap” and “not something intended for longevity.”

COBOL, refined and tweaked over the years, is still used, especially in banking and finance. More than $1 trillion a day in transactions are executed on systems running COBOL code.

The hurry-up culture of the software industry, technology experts say, with its emphasis on creating new products contributes to computing complexity and risk. And while there have been dramatic episodes recently of artificial intelligence agents going rogue and breaking into computer networks, the experts note that the Microsoft and F.A.A. cases were old-fashioned technology lapses, not the mischief of malicious hackers.

Jen Easterly, a former director of the U.S. Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency, made that point in a recent guest essay in The New York Times.

“The United States does not have a cybersecurity problem so much as a software quality problem,” Ms. Easterly wrote. “Much of the multibillion-dollar cybersecurity industry exists to compensate for technology built for speed, convenience and features — not security.”

There are start-ups deploying cutting-edge technology to address that shortcoming. Will Wilson, a former software engineer at Google and Apple, is the chief executive of one such venture. His company, Antithesis, is building A.I. models that simulate software and hardware systems in detail to spot potential problems — like the ones suffered by Microsoft and the F.A.A.

“Sometimes the low-level detail really matters,” Mr. Wilson said. “And you don’t notice until the system comes crashing down.”

Pursuing an A.I. solution seems its own paradox. The technology makes software easier to write, automating broad swaths of programming and further enlarging the digital universe. The leading A.I. models are so complex that even the scientists creating them don’t fully understand how they work. This is the tool being proposed to overcome the challenge of technology fragility.

“A.I. is our only hope,” said Michael Cusumano, a professor at MIT’s Sloan School of Management. “These technology systems are so complex they are beyond the ability of any human to analyze them.”
